title: What is makhana? A short guide to the lotus seed snack
excerpt: Where makhana comes from, how it is popped, and why it has moved from festival kitchens to everyday snacking.
body:
Makhana, also called fox nut or phool makhana, is the popped seed of the prickly water lily, Euryale ferox. The plant grows in still ponds and wetlands, and most of India's crop comes from the ponds of Bihar.

From pond to pop

The seeds are gathered from the pond bed, washed, sun-dried and graded by size. They are then roasted in an iron pan and struck with a mallet, so the hard shell cracks and the white kernel puffs out. That light, airy puff is the makhana you know.

Why it has become a favourite snack

  • It is light and crunchy, with a mild taste that takes on seasoning well.
  • Lotus seeds are naturally gluten-free.
  • Roasted makhana has a good share of protein and fibre for a crunchy snack.

For generations makhana was a fasting and festival food, slow-cooked into kheer or curries. Today, dry-roasted and seasoned, it has become an everyday snack for the desk, the drive home and the evening chai.

How Vohra's makes it

We dry-roast premium graded makhana with a little rice bran oil, season each batch with one of seven flavour blends, and seal it in a 100 g tin so the crunch survives the trip to your door.

title: Roasted, not fried: what it means for your snack
excerpt: Why we dry-roast our makhana with a little rice bran oil, and what to look for on the label of any crunchy snack.
body:
Many crunchy snacks get their crunch from deep frying. Makhana does not need it. Its puffed structure is already light and crisp, so a slow dry roast is enough to bring out the crunch.

How we roast

Each batch is roasted slowly with a small amount of rice bran oil, just enough to help the seasoning stick. The result is a light, airy bite rather than a heavy, oily one.

Reading the label

Whatever snack you pick, the nutrition table tells the real story. A few things worth checking:

  • Total and saturated fat per 100 g, and per serve.
  • Sodium, especially in strongly seasoned flavours.
  • Added sugar, which can hide in tangy and sweet blends.
  • Protein and fibre, which help a snack feel more satisfying.

Every Vohra's product page lists full ingredients, the complete nutrition table and allergen advice, exactly as printed on the tin.

title: Seven flavours, one tin: how to pick yours
excerpt: From classic Pink Salt to fiery Peri Peri, a quick guide to the Vohra's range by mood and taste.
body:
Our seven flavours fall into four simple families. Here is how to find your favourite.

Classic & light

Start with Pink Salt if you want to taste the makhana itself, or Pink Salt & Black Pepper for a gentle warmth.

Spicy & tangy

Peri Peri brings real heat, while Tangy Tomato is bright and zesty.

Creamy & cheesy

Cream & Onion and Cheesy Delight are rich, comforting and very easy to finish in one sitting.

Fresh & herby

Mint Pudina is cool and refreshing, a good match for a hot afternoon.

Still can't decide? The tasting set on our shop page adds one tin of every flavour in a single tap.

title: Festive gifting with makhana: simple ideas that look good
excerpt: Tins, hampers and office gifting ideas for Diwali and beyond, using the full Vohra's range.
body:
Dry fruits have always been the heart of Indian festive gifting. Roasted makhana is a lighter, modern addition, and our tins are made to be given.

The tasting set

One tin of each of our seven flavours makes a colourful, ready-made gift. It suits families who like to share and try everything.

Pair it with dry fruits

Coming from Khari Baoli, we love a mixed hamper: a few makhana tins alongside almonds, cashews or raisins in a simple basket or box.

Office and bulk gifting

For teams, clients or events, a single flavour or a mix of tins works well and is easy to ship. Get in touch with us for bulk and corporate orders.

A small tip

Tins keep makhana crisp, but once opened, close the lid tightly and finish within a few days for the best crunch.
